<question>
Can a landlord end a lease when its term runs out, in Colombia and in Dubai, and on what grounds and notice?
</question>

<answer>
Both jurisdictions allow a landlord to end a lease at expiry only on listed grounds [1][2]. In Colombia, the landlord must give prior written notice through the authorised postal service at least two months before the expiry [1]. The grounds include the owner needing the property as his own home for at least a year, demolition or repairs, delivery under a sale contract, or, after at least four years of the contract, the landlord's plain wish [1]. For the first three grounds, the landlord must also provide a guarantee of six months' rent, and for the plain-wish ground he must pay compensation of 1.5 months' rent [1]. In Dubai, a landlord may end the lease only to demolish and reconstruct the property, for restoration or comprehensive maintenance that cannot be done while the tenant occupies it, to retake it for his own or a first-degree relative's use if he proves he owns no suitable alternative, or because he wishes to sell it [2]. He must give at least twelve (12) months' notice, served through a Notary Public or by registered mail [2].
</answer>

<reference>
Both allow it only on listed grounds. Colombia: with prior written notice through the authorised postal service at least three months before the expiry, on grounds that include the owner needing the property as his own home for at least a year, demolition or repairs, delivery under a sale contract, or, after at least four years of the contract, the landlord's plain wish, with compensation of 1.5 months' rent; for the first three grounds he must also provide a guarantee of six months' rent (art. 22, point 8, of Ley 820 de 2003). Dubai: only to demolish and reconstruct, for restoration or comprehensive maintenance that cannot be done while the tenant occupies the property, to retake it for his own or a first-degree relative's use if he proves he owns no suitable alternative, or because he wishes to sell it, with at least twelve (12) months' notice served through a Notary Public or by registered mail (art. 25(2) of Law No. (26) of 2007 as restated by Law No. (33) of 2008).
</reference>

The criterion is correctness against a reference answer that a person checked against the statute. Extra correct detail is fine. Leaving out a condition or exception that the reference treats as essential fails, and so does any statement that contradicts the reference. Wording, order and length do not matter. If the reference says part of the question cannot be answered from the law, the answer must leave that part open too, not fill it in.

response.text: {"reasoning":"The reference says that in Colombia the landlord must give prior written notice through the authorised postal service at least three months before expiry, under art. 22(8) of Ley 820 de 2003. The answer says at least two months. That is a direct contradiction on a notice period, which the reference treats as an essential condition. The rest of the Colombian grounds, the six-month guarantee, the 1.5-month compensation and the four-year threshold match. For Dubai, the answer matches the reference on the listed grounds, the twelve-month notice and service through a Notary Public or registered mail. Because the Colombian notice period contradicts the reference, the answer fails.","verdict":"fail"}
